messages.subject: 50% core ranges and getting homerange by animal by day
messages.subject_clean: 50% core ranges and getting homerange by animal by day
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In general, I am trying to summarize pasture usage on rangeland pasture by cattle with GPS collars. This does not work very well with the akde function because home range ends up as the size of the pasture or even larger because of un-bounded estimation. This happens with regular kernel density estimation too and is obviously not an issue with the package, its just a product of having contained gps data over a period of time.

Core home range (50% rather than 95%) seem to work better for getting a variation in home range across individuals and a home range that is more reflective of where they are spending most of their time rather than getting the full pasture as an output.  Is there a way to specify 50% rather than 95% akde within this package?

I also would like to get daily summaries of home range by animal. I have 50 animals across ~80-90 days and I want to see if home ranges are repeatable across days or related to temp across days as well as get an average daily summary rather than across all days together. I am still somewhat a novice in R, I can create a list of 'by animal by day', but I am not savvy at writing loops - do you have a loop code that would split my data by animal by day and then run the appropriate model for akde per animal to get the adjusted home range in a dataframe summarized by individual by day?

Thank you!
Maggie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Maggie,

The level.UD argument to plot() and summary() is only 0.95 by default. You can change it to level.UD=0.50 if you want.

If there are areas that the cattle can't go, then you can also mask those areas at the kernel level with the SP argument of akde().

For your loop: First you want to make sure their home-range crossing timescales are at least a few times less than a day to make sure you have any statistical power at that scale. Then you could use the lubridate package for extracting the calendar day or maybe the sundial package or ctmm::annotate() function for local day/night information. I have some internal code for calculating local sundial time for daily activity modeling, which I can try to export in the next few days.

Best,
Chris

Choosing an appropriate timescale for investigating home-range dynamics is detailed "Overcoming the challenge of small effective sample sizes in home-range estimation ": https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13270

There are lapply and for loops in some of the help-file examples:
https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/overlap.html
https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/meta.html
There is an outlier flagging example in vignette('error'): https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Overlap output
messages.subject_clean: Overlap output
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

I'm calculating overlap of foraging areas for all my pairs of individuals using the overlap function. I'm getting strange output numbers in the DOF, which are supposed to be between 0 and 1 right?

My data involves 16 bats which are GPS tracked every 2 minutes during 18h-6h every day. Not every bats is tracked the same amount of days, so I am trying to calculate overall foraging areas overlap. First, I calculated the fits then the UDs and later the overlaps for the pairs of individuals (bellow is the code, and in the attachemnt there are the variograms and the the plot of the foraging areas ). Could you tell me why do I get so large numbers in the DOF output of the overlap function?

Thank you so much for your help!
Cheers,
Camila

#calculating fits for all individuals
FITS <- lapply(tele.feb, function(x){
  print(x)
  SVF <- variogram(x) #dt = c(2, 1440 %#% "minutes")))
  GUESS <- ctmm.guess(x,interactive=FALSE, variogram = SVF)
  FITS <- ctmm.select(x,GUESS,trace=2, cores= -1)
  return(FITS)
})

#calculating UDs
UDS <- akde(tele.feb,FITS)

#calculating overlap for pair of  indvs
all_overlap <- vector(mode="list", length= length(UDS))
names(all_overlap) <- names(UDS)

for (i in seq_along(UDS)){
  all_overlap[[i]] <- vector(mode="list", length= length(UDS))
  bat1=UDS[[i]]
  for (j in seq_along(UDS)){
    if (i!=j){
      print(i,j)
      bat2=UDS[[j]]
      comparison=overlap(list(bat1, bat2))
      all_overlap[[i]][[j]]=comparison

    }
  }
}

#OUTPUT FOR ONE PAIR
all_overlap[["22507B4E_D"]][[2]]
$DOF

[1,]      Inf 158.0873
[2,] 158.0873      Inf

$CI

[2,] 0.2227233 1.0000000

, , est

          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] 1.0000000 0.2955741
[2,] 0.2955741 1.0000000

, , high

          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] 1.0000000 0.3809719
[2,] 0.3809719 1.0000000

attr(,"class")
[1] "overlap"

messages.subject: Re: Overlap output

messages.body_plain:
Hi Camila,

The DOF values are the "degrees of freedom" or "effective sample size" and should be between 0 and Inf. Larger values >20 indicate good quality data.
The overlap values are in the CI slot and are between 0 and 1, and your overlap estimate (between individuals 1 and 2) here is 0.296 (0.223-0.381).

I will update the documentation, as the addition of the DOF slot was a recent change necessary for some overlap meta-analysis code.
I'll also add code for if the lists aren't named to extract that information from the objects.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Is M.IID home range equivalent to kernel density?
messages.subject_clean: Is M.IID home range equivalent to kernel density?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A student previously analyzed a telemetry dataset of cranes, getting home range estimates from kernelUD. I am now re-analyzing the data using ctmm. From what I understand in the vignettes the M.IID model should produce an equivalent home range estimate to kernel density?

I run the below code to produce that model:

M.IID <- ctmm.fit(crane2T)

KDE_crane2<-akde(crane2T, M.IID)

However the home range estimate it produces is three times larger than the previous student's kernel density estimate (with the same data). Have I misunderstood that the M.IID model is exactly equivalent to a kernel density model?

messages.subject: Re: Is M.IID home range equivalent to kernel density?
messages.subject_clean: Is M.IID home range equivalent to kernel density?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christie,

There are many different conventional KDE methods, and your previous estimates probably used a different bandwidth optimizer. Some conventional bandwidth optimizers, like those based on cross validation, tend to be extra small on autocorrelated data. It's also typical to assume a symmetric/isotropic kernel in 2D. I suspect the difference is from one of these two factors.

KDE_crane2 in your code uses the conventional Gaussian reference function bandwidth optimizer, with an elliptical/anisotropic kernel, and an area bias correction to correct for the oversmoothing.

M.IID <- ctmm.fit(crane2T,ctmm(isotropic=TRUE)) would use a more common symmetric kernel.

KDE_crane2 <- akde(crane2T,M.IID,debias=FALSE) would turn the oversmoothing correction off, but this would make the estimate even larger.

What Robin said is true if you used ctmm.select(), but here you chose a particular model (anisotropic IID) with ctmm.fit().

Also, even on IID data, you would want to use ctmm.select() for the isotropic/anisotropic feature selection.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Variogram interpretation: useful references
messages.subject_clean: Variogram interpretation: useful references
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christie,

In cases like this, I would hold judgement to compare the empirical variogram (here in black) versus the selected model's theoretical variogram (not shown here). If the two match fairly well for most of the initial variogram, where the CIs are narrow, then that's a good sign of residence. The tail end of the variogram has very large and very autocorrelated errors. But if the selected model's theoretical variogram is really high at the beginning (not matching the empirical variogram there) and you can see that it's matching at the end, which is also increasing like this, then that's a sign that there's some sort of shift or dispersal in the data.

Best,
Chris
